findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the post-rollback re-convergence path for clones that already reconciled onto the rewritten baseline (assert on client state AFTER revert, not only that the backup ref is restored).
evidence: 'Rollback: immutable backup ref refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date> ... the swap is one revertible step'
'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline (append-only files, not history merge)'

ABSENCE: no assertion on how clones that already reconciled onto the new baseline re-converge if the swap is reverted — rollback 'completes' but leaves reconciled clients interpreting a graph that was reverted away
findings.finding: The plan's rollback design asserts the swap is revertible (restore backup ref / S3 rollback bundle prefix) but does not assert on the STATE of clients that already reconciled onto the rewritten baseline AFTER a rollback. Post-swap, clients reconcile by event-file replay onto the NEW baseline (new commit SHAs); if the swap is then rolled back to the pre-reclaim history, those already-reconciled clones are left pointing at a baseline/SHA graph that no longer exists on the remote, with no stated re-convergence path.
findings.location: Risk / rollback section; Feasibility 'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline'
scenarios: Swap succeeds, several active clones reconcile onto the new baseline, then a defect is found and the operator reverts to the backup ref; those clones now diverge from the restored pre-reclaim history
findings.suggested_fix: Add a rollback acceptance step: after restoring the backup ref, define how reconciled clones detect the reverted head (stale-clone/S3 override path) and re-replay their event files onto the restored history, and bound the window during which reconciliation is deferred until rollback is ruled out.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State explicitly which lever turns the Verify Authorship gate green at the pack limit (W3 raise vs. the rewrite), and quantify the residual pack size after the N=30d rewrite against the (possibly re-set) budget, so the destructive rewrite's contribution to the named bug is unambiguous.
evidence: Plan: 'Max safe win N=30d ≈ 365–380 MiB; ... ≤100 MiB needs an unsafe <4-day horizon. A temporary budget-raise bridge (W3) is unavoidable'
Bug a453 AC requires 'evidence of a passing Verify Authorship Identity run' against REBAR_CHECKOUT_PACK_LIMIT_KIB=102400 (verify-identity.yml:47)
The rewrite reduces ~365–380 MiB from a ~481 MiB pack, leaving ~100–116 MiB — at/over the current 100 MiB limit, so W3 (raise) is what actually clears the gate
findings.finding: By the plan's own quantification the destructive history-rewrite does not, at any safe horizon, bring the blobless pack under the 100 MiB budget that the named bug requires; the gate is actually made green by the W3 budget-raise bridge, not by the rewrite. The plan should make explicit which lever resolves the named problem (a green Verify Authorship Identity run at the pack limit) so the high-blast-radius rewrite is justified against its actual contribution.
findings.location: 'Quantified win — insufficient alone' section and Acceptance Criteria ('Pack-shrink quantified... against the 100 MiB budget')
scenarios: Reviewer/operator asks 'does the rewrite make the CI gate green?' — the answer is 'only combined with a W3 limit raise', which is not stated as a success criterion
A later child slice executes the destructive rewrite yet the gate stays red because W3 was not also applied

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Evaluate and explicitly accept/reject CI-side partial clone (--filter=tree:0) and/or shallow --depth on verify-identity.yml as prior-art alternatives to the destructive history rewrite, given trees are ~95% of bytes and the budget lives at the checkout layer.
evidence: Plan asserts: 'The only lever is reducing reachable commit/tree objects on tickets history — causally-safe history reclamation'
Plan: 'the blobless CI checkout pack is ~481 MiB vs a deliberate 100 MiB budget (verify-identity.yml:47)' — checkout already uses --filter=blob:none but no deeper tree filter is considered
Plan: 'trees ≈95% of bytes' — --filter=tree:0 partial clone omits trees at fetch time, directly on-point

Retrieved (github.blog 'Get up to speed with partial clone and shallow clone'): blobless (--filter=blob:none) vs treeless (--filter=tree:0) vs shallow are stacking fetch-time levers that narrow trees/commits without altering server history
ABSENCE: plan proves git gc/repack does not shrink the pack but does not evaluate or reject a CI-checkout-layer tree:0 / shallow-depth fetch as an alternative or bridge to the destructive rewrite
findings.finding: The novel destructive history-rewrite architecture is chosen to shrink the CI checkout pack without considering the well-trodden CI-side prior art (partial clone --filter=tree:0 and/or shallow --depth) that targets exactly the measured cost — trees at ~95% of bytes — at fetch time, on the same verify-identity.yml the budget lives in, without rewriting authoritative shared history.
findings.location: Why / Quantified win / Mechanism sections; AC 'Coalescing shown insufficient alone at any safe horizon'
scenarios: CI checkout only needs the tip working tree for verify-authorship, so a tree:0 or shallow fetch could hit the 100 MiB budget without any horizon-based history reclamation and without the accepted >N-day clone data-loss
If tree:0/shallow gets CI under budget, the entire destructive-rewrite epic (and its >N-day loss acceptance) may be unnecessary or reducible to the deferred W1/W2 structural fixes
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Rejected alternatives' subsection that measures a --filter=tree:0 (and/or shallow-depth) CI checkout against the 100 MiB budget and states why it is insufficient or unusable for verify-authorship's needs; if it suffices, prefer it (or use it as the W3 bridge) over the destructive rewrite.
